nameStory: The 'swamp' in this damselfly's name comes from its preference for wetlands with lots of vegetation - the marshy, boggy areas where cattails and sedges grow thick. 'Spreadwing' refers to how these damselflies hold their wings when they rest - unlike most damselflies that fold their wings back along their body, spreadwings hold them out at angles like tiny airplane wings.
description: The Swamp Spreadwing is a delicate damselfly that grows about 2 inches long, making it one of the larger damselflies you'll encounter in New England wetlands. Like all damselflies, it has a slender body and four wings of roughly equal size, but what makes spreadwings special is how they hold their wings partially open when perched. These graceful insects are expert hunters, snatching mosquitoes and other small flying insects right out of the air with their spiny legs. You'll spot them from late spring through fall, often perched on emergent plants around the edges of marshes and swamps.

idTips.label: Wing position at rest
idTips.description: Wings held partially spread at angles when perched, not folded flat against the body like most damselflies - this gives them their 'spreadwing' name and is immediately noticeable

idTips.label: Body size
idTips.description: Noticeably robust for a damselfly at nearly 2 inches long - feels substantial if you gently catch one, unlike the more delicate smaller damselflies

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Almost always found around vegetated wetlands with emergent plants like cattails and sedges - rarely seen far from marshy areas

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Strong, purposeful flight with less fluttering than smaller damselflies - you can hear a subtle whirring sound from their wings in close encounters

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often perches vertically on plant stems with head up, wings spread - stays relatively still and approachable compared to skittish dragonflies

habitat: Look for Swamp Spreadwings around vegetated wetlands throughout New England - marshes, swamps, bog edges, and pond margins with plenty of emergent plants like cattails, sedges, and rushes. They prefer areas with both open water and dense vegetation, from sea level up into the mountains. You'll often find them in the same spots where Red-winged Blackbirds nest and Great Blue Herons hunt.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with peak activity starting in early June. Look for fresh individuals with pristine wings perched on new marsh vegetation growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak season through July and August when adults are most active and numerous. This is the best time to observe mating behavior and egg-laying in vegetated shallows.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active well into September and even early October in warm years. Late-season individuals may show wing wear and faded colors from months of activity.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - they spend winter as eggs laid in plant stems, waiting for spring warmth to trigger development into aquatic nymphs.

funFact: Swamp Spreadwing females have a tiny saw-like structure called an ovipositor that they use to slice open plant stems underwater, then back up and deposit their eggs inside the cut - essentially performing underwater surgery while holding their breath!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spreadwing species, but habitat is your best clue - Swamp Spreadwings stick to vegetated wetlands while many relatives prefer more open water. Remember: 'Swamp Spreadwings love swamps' - if you're in cattail marshes rather than open ponds, you're likely looking at the right species.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'damselfly' comes from their delicate, graceful appearance compared to the more robust dragonflies - think of a medieval damsel versus a knight in armor. Despite the dainty name, these are fierce predators that catch nearly 100% of the prey they pursue, making them more successful hunters than sharks or lions.
compareHints: Among New England's nine Lestes species, Swamp Spreadwings are distinguished by their strong preference for heavily vegetated wetlands and their larger, more robust build. While Emerald Spreadwings prefer open ponds and Northern Spreadwings like temporary pools, Swamp Spreadwings are the cattail marsh specialists. Their size and habitat preference make them one of the easier spreadwings to identify with confidence.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's spreadwings, the Slender Spreadwing is distinguished by its exceptionally thin body profile and pale blue face coloration.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Spotted Spreadwing is one of the easier ones to identify thanks to its distinctive wing spots.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Amber-winged is distinguished by its wing coloration when present, though this can be subtle.
Among New England's spreadwings, the elegant spreadwing is distinguished by its bronze-brown coloration and medium size.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Northern Spreadwing is distinguished by its preference for more permanent water bodies compared to species like the Swamp Spreadwing which favors temporary pools.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Emerald Spreadwing stands out for its brilliant metallic green coloration - most others like the Swamp Spreadwing appear more bronze or brown.
Among New England spreadwings, sweetflag spreadwings are distinguished by their preference for heavily vegetated wetlands rather than open water.
